title: Husband calls for PM to intervene after wife detained in Egypt
content:
The husband of a woman who was detained by the Egyptian authorities has called for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to get involved and help with her release.
Eman el-Shazly, from Handsworth Wood, in Birmingham, was taken from her mother's house in Cairo two months ago, allegedly in relation to her sister's online activism.
Her husband, Zeesharn Moustapha, said that their family felt "very helpless" and that their "only possible solution" was for Burnham to "make a phone call to Egypt" to end the detainment.
The BBC has approached the Egyptian consulate in London for a response. The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said it was in contact with authorities in Egypt.
Moustapha said he had had "no contact whatsoever" with his wife, but had heard from her mother that her health had deteriorated due to a lack of food and medical assistance.
"It's not a five-star hotel, there's 30 individuals sleeping in a cell with one toilet and one shower," he said.
He told the BBC that his wife had travelled to Egypt to look after her elderly, sick mother, who had been undertaking 18-hour round trips to take food to el-Shazly's two brothers in detention.
The 46-year-old claimed his wife had been detained due to her sister's online posts from the UK targeting  the Egyptian leadership,
"How somebody can make videos abroad knowing it's causing direct consequences to people abroad, what kind of person can sleep at night doing that," he said.
Her sister told the BBC that she was sorry that her family had been detained. She said this was a tactic used by the Egyptian government to silence critics.
But she would not stop posting her videos, because she felt it was her duty to make a stand.
Moustapha described support from the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) as "useless" with no calls or updates from them.
"We are very angry, we feel that the government isn't doing anything to secure the release of a British citizen," he said, adding that his wife had held a British passport for 20 years.
Moustapha, who has four children, said there was no evidence against his wife, who was being left "to rot in jail" and that it was a "clear example of collective punishment".
"The kids are very distraught, they are suffering, they've lost their mother at the moment and we genuinely don't know what to do about it," he said.
A spokesperson for the FCDO said: "We are supporting the family of a British national detained in Egypt, and are in contact with the authorities."

title: There's a crackdown on sports piracy - but is it already out of control?
content:
"Football's Gone Round the Spend!" screamed The People newspaper one Sunday in July 1995. It reported breathlessly that three clubs between them were set to pay out more than £20m on new players.
The highlight that summer was the transfer of Stan Collymore from Nottingham Forest to Liverpool for a British record fee of £8.5m.
That number might not seem too impressive today, in an age when £100m transfers are almost commonplace. But at the time it was seismic stuff, and it symbolised the conversion of football from sport into big business.
All of this had been made possible in the early 1990s by the creation of the Premier League, and its initial TV deal with the broadcaster Sky, which paid more than £300m for five years of rights. The agreement put live top-tier football behind a TV paywall for the first time.
It was a lucrative model, one that other leading championships in motorsport, rugby, golf and cricket would later seek to replicate.
But now, that model is coming under pressure. Piracy has become endemic in British sports: around half of sports fans now admit to using what they might euphemistically call "alternative" means to watch paywalled material, according to the consultancy Ampere Analysis.
And this summer saw signs of a clampdown.
In August, a man in Lancashire was jailed for six and a half years for running an illegal streaming service that police said had generated almost £1m in illicit profits. In June, a postman from Pembrokeshire was jailed for over three years for selling illegal subscriptions and supplying pirate software to nearly 2,000 people.
A third man, from Merseyside, received a suspended 32-month sentence in August for similar offences. Several pubs have been fined thousands of pounds for screening matches illegally.
TV companies that have paid huge sums for exclusive rights to high-profile sports are having to work harder than ever to protect their investments. To some extent, broadcasters used to see copyright theft as a cost of doing business: irritating and expensive, but not an existential threat. But now, as advertising revenues fall, and viewers move away from long-term subscription services like Sky or TNT Sports, the industry is getting seriously worried.
There is a great deal at stake. The Premier League alone is a sporting monster. In its most recent deal, it sold its viewing rights to domestic audiences for £6.7bn over four years, with almost as much coming from foreign rights. Armed with bundles of TV cash, clubs have been able to attract the finest players in the world. That in turn has given the league a major international profile.
Although football has been the main beneficiary of paid-for TV in the UK, other competitions such as Formula One, Six Nations rugby and the Wimbledon tennis championships have also commanded very high fees for selling exclusive rights. Live sport on free-to-air television has become increasingly rare.
Yet that wealth could be threatened by a surge in piracy and illegal viewing. The practice is most common among younger, digital-native audiences, who each year become a larger and larger share of sports fans. But many older viewers also seem comfortable with it.
"For 18 to 34-year-olds, it's over 70% who admit to doing this regularly," says Daniel Monaghan, a researcher at Ampere Analysis. "Over half of 35 to 44s admit to doing it, and about a third of those aged 45 to 64."
This year's Champions League final went behind a paywall in the UK for the first time in more than 30 years. Viewers were asked to pay at least £4.99 to watch it, prompting a backlash, including from the then-prime minister, Arsenal fan Sir Keir Starmer.
"Hardworking people shouldn't have to fork out for a subscription to watch this match," he wrote on X.
Many simply refused to pay: 3.7 million IP addresses accessed illegal streams of the match in the UK, according to research carried out by the Gaming Compliance International consultancy, on behalf of the Guardian newspaper. That compared to around seven million people who watched it legally in the UK.
One prolific user of pirate streams is "Kiran", a tech sector worker in his 30s, who prefers not to give his real name. A keen Arsenal fan, he likes to watch Premier League and Champions League games, as well as big matches in Spain's La Liga. He has a paid subscription to TNT Sports, but uses streaming websites to see games that are not available there.
"What it comes down to is the financial side - that's the big one - and ease of access as well," he says. "Getting every single game will cost you hundreds of pounds a year."
Meanwhile the streams he uses are free, with links readily obtainable on social media.

The article highlights the importance of protecting these investments and the potential consequences of a surge in piracy and illegal viewing.

title: The playground murder: Trauma, loss and a love that endured
content:
When Diane Watson was stabbed to death in the playground of a Glasgow school in 1991, her best friend Pauline was standing by her side.
Pauline watched as 16-year-old Diane collapsed after the knife attack by another pupil and then helped to carry her across the road to the arms of her parents who lived in an upstairs flat within view of the school.
Diane's murder would not only devastate her family, her friends and the local community, its shockwaves would go on to be felt for decades.
Warning - this story contains descriptions of violence, death and suicide.
Thirty-five years later, Pauline Love Thomson has spoken for the first time about the trauma of that April morning when she was just 16.
In a new BBC Scotland podcast, Crime Next Door: The Playground Murder , she relives the day 15-year-old Barbara Glover came to Whitehill secondary school in Glasgow's east end armed with a large kitchen knife.
Pauline describes how a large crowd of schoolkids gathered round as Glover shouted at Diane while waving the knife - and the chilling moment she dealt the deadly blow.
"She actually let out a growl when she stepped forward," Pauline says.
"She stabbed her and people started just moving away. Everybody just vanished.
"I went over, I just put my arm around her [Diane's] shoulder because I hadn't actually appreciated the damage that the knife would have done. It was a big knife."
Pauline tried to help her bleeding friend get home to the flat across the road she shared with her mum, dad and brother Alan.
She recalls Diane saying: "I don't believe it. She stabbed me."
It was only a short distance to the flat but Pauline felt her friend slumping even before they reached the school gate.
With the help of two other girls she got Diane across the road but by the time she reached the entrance to the flat, she collapsed.
Her father Jim, who had been alerted by another girl battering on his door, ran down and took his daughter in his arms.
He carried her upstairs and desperately tried to revive her as her mother Margaret and 15-year-old brother looked on in horror.
Jim tried to give her mouth-to-mouth resuscitation, Pauline said.
"I'm shouting, 'you're not doing it right'," she said.
"I could hear her gurgling. There was blood coming out her mouth."
Diane Watson was later declared dead at Glasgow Royal Infirmary and Barbara Glover handed herself into the police.
